The spatial model predicts each selection from:

  - distance to the last item (`rho_delta`),
  - direction relative to the last move (`rho_psi`),
  - absolute direction (`fourier_coef`).

The multi-level version, used whenever the data have more than one
person, gives each person their own parameter values (`u_*`) around the
condition values, with between-person SDs (`sigma_u_*`).

We simulate six people with known parameters, fit the model, and check it
recovers them.

Code: `spatial.R`.

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::read_chunk("spatial.R")
```

```{r load}
```

## Simulate

Six people, $K = 2$ conditions, 10 trials per person and condition, on a
7 $\times$ 7 grid with a quarter of cells empty.

```{r stimuli}
```

The conditions differ in every parameter:

- Condition *one*: weaker distance attraction (0.75), turning back
  ($-1$), and moves mostly along the four cardinal directions;
- Condition *two*: stronger distance attraction (1.5), carrying on (1),
  and a strong rightward bias.

Each person's values vary around these condition values. The simulation
draws each between-person SD from an exponential with rate `sd_lambda`
(a larger rate means less spread between people), then each person's
values.

```{r simulate_params}
```

As in the single-level example, we prepare the data and pass it to the
*simulate* version of our Stan model:

```{r sim_stan_list}
```

```{r simulate}
```

The simulation selects every item, but real foragers often stop early, so
`truncate_trials()` drops a few selections from the end of each trial: a
Poisson(2) number of them, always keeping at least 10. The dropped items
stay on the display, unselected. This allows us to test that our model
handles inexhaustive data without problems.

```{r truncate}
```

By default `plot_trial()` plots one randomly selected trial per condition.

```{r fig-trial}
#| fig-cap: "One simulated trial from each condition: items and selection order."
```

```{r fig-steps}
#| fig-cap: "Distance and direction of moves in the simulated data."
```

We can compute a number of trial stats for comparing against the fitted
model's posterior predictions. With several people they are averaged to
one row per person and condition, as single trials are noisy.

```{r trial-stats}
```

We also keep each person's simulated values, to check the per-person
estimates against later:

```{r groundtruth}
```

## Fit

We now fit the multi-level spatial version of FoMo to our simulated data.
Four chains of `r n_iter` warmup and `r n_iter` sampling iterations.

*Note*: by default the per-person distance effects are centred
(`centred_params`, see `prep_stan_list()`). With only 10 trials per
person that sometimes gives divergent transitions (0 and 22 on two
datasets simulated like this one, against none without centring), so here
none are centred (`centred_params = "none"`). The multi-level cat page
shows the same check for that model.

```{r fit_prep}
#| results: hide
```

```{r fit}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr rlang::hash(list(sl, n_iter))
#| results: hide
```

## Diagnostics

Posterior medians and 97% HPDIs, the values the data were simulated from
(`true`, and whether each is `inside` its HPDI), and convergence (R-hat,
ESS), for the fixed effects and the between-person SDs (`sigma_u_*`).
Each person's values (`u_*`) are summarised in one row per parameter.
About one in 33 simulation values should fall outside its HPDI by chance;
with six people the SDs are hard to pin down. R-hat above 1.01, or a bulk
or tail ESS in the low hundreds, means the chains haven't mixed well
enough to trust the tails of the posterior. The summary's last line names
the worst parameter (random effects included); the table colours R-hat
and ESS green (good), orange (acceptable) or red (bad).

```{r fit-summary}
#| results: asis
```

Rank plots of the five worst-mixing parameters, judged by R-hat and ESS
together. Each histogram shows where one chain's draws rank among all the
draws: if the chains have mixed well, every chain's histogram is roughly
flat and they overlap.

```{r fig-traces}
#| fig-cap: "Rank plots of the five worst-mixing parameters, coloured green (good), orange (acceptable) or red (bad) by their R-hat and ESS."
```

`log_lik` is one value per trial, so loo leaves out a whole trial at a
time. A Pareto k above 0.7 marks a trial the fit leans on heavily, whose
loo estimate is unreliable. `check_high_pareto_k()` lists those trials,
worst first, with the person each belongs to (`z`).

```{r loo}
```

## Posterior

### Posterior densities

Where a posterior sits well inside its prior band, the data rather than
the prior set the estimate. A posterior pressed against the edge of its
band means the prior is doing some of the work.

```{r fig-post}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Posterior densities by condition. Grey bands: prior HPDIs; dashed lines: simulation values."
```

### Each person

Per-person estimates are pulled towards the condition value (shrinkage),
most for people whose own data say least. So a person's interval can
miss an extreme simulation value even when the condition values are
recovered.

```{r fig-person-spatial}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Each person's $\\rho_\\delta$ and $\\rho_\\psi$: posterior intervals, simulation values (squares) and condition-level HPDIs (shaded)."
```

### Accuracy

- Deterministic accuracy: how often the item the model judges most likely
is the one selected.
- Probability of the chosen item: the probability the
model gave the item that was selected, averaged over selections; it
credits the model for being nearly right, not only for top picks.
- Chance (1 / items left) rises through a trial as fewer items remain.
- The nearest-neighbour baseline always picks the closest remaining
item, so the gap above it is what the model adds to proximity alone.

*Note*: this is in-sample accuracy, which overestimates out-of-sample accuracy.

```{r fig-accuracy}
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy of the model's predictions at each selection, with chance and nearest-neighbour baselines."
```

## Posterior predictive check

The model doesn't predict when a trial stops,
so each simulated trial keeps as many selections as the data have.

```{r sim-posterior}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr rlang::hash(list(sl, n_iter, n_post_draws))
```

```{r fig-sim-trial}
#| fig-cap: "One trial per condition, simulated from the fitted model."
```

Finally, we compare the trial statistics between the training data and data simulated from the fitted posterior. As none of the trial statistics are model parameters, reproducing them tests whether the fitted model captures aspects of the behaviour it was not fitted to directly.

```{r fig-sim-stats}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr rlang::hash(list(found_post, trial_stats))
#| fig-cap: "Trial statistics per person for the fitted data (x) and data simulated from the posterior (y). Points near the diagonal mean the model reproduces them."
```
